findings.message: Skills practised: the story practises decoding FLOSS words (fall, chill, pass, cliff, mess, grass, spill, class, cross, small) and initial-blend words (trail, storm, frost, sled, crack, slope, bright, snow, climb, track, drift) in natural sentences, repeated across every branch rather than drilled as a list. Readers build sequencing by following an ordered rescue plan (splint the ankle, ration the food, scout or search, cross the gap, choose an ending), inference by reading the crack-line clue and the bent-pole item to judge whether crossing the gap is safe, vocabulary from context through the glossary entries and in-text explanations (e.g. "It is a sprain, not a break"), and comprehension through branching choices whose consequences depend on earlier decisions. The five endings and recurring clue/item mechanics also give sustained engagement and rereading value.

Automated-detection limits: the literacy report's concept and word-set checks (and my own spot check against src/literacy/taxonomy.ts) match spelling patterns, not sounds, so they cannot confirm pronunciation, syllable stress or true decodability for a given child's program. For example the FLOSS and initial-blend detectors would flag a word with the right letters even if it were pronounced differently; a human structured-literacy tutor should still confirm the phonological claims for the specific learner before use.

Independent concept-match check (requested because a sibling job, job-20261118-lock-in-at-castellan-hal-3d1b03, had a concept/word mismatch in its brief): I hand-checked every word in brief.json's wordSets against the detectors in src/literacy/taxonomy.ts. floss-words (fall, chill, pass, cliff, mess, grass, spill, class, cross, small) are each single-syllable with a short vowel + doubled ff/ll/ss at the end, matching the floss detector (vowelGroups length 1 and /[aeiou](ff|ll|ss|zz)$/). initial-blend-words (trail, storm, frost, sled, crack, slope, bright, snow, climb, track, drift) each start with one of the listed two-letter blends followed immediately by a vowel, matching the initial-blend detector. No mismatches found; this brief does not repeat the sibling job's defect. This agrees with the automated report's word-set-concepts-match-spelling check (ok, no mismatches).

"small" is reused heavily (14 of the floss set's 37 total occurrences, e.g. "a small ranger shelter" in climax-approach, "a small ranger station" in ending-3, "small details" in ending-1, "small, even shares" in ration-the-food) because it doubles as a generic adjective. It still reads naturally everywhere I checked, but the narrative designer could trade one or two instances for a currently under-used set word (spill and drift each appear only once) if a future revision wants more variety.

shelfSummary.blurb: When a snow slide traps Vale, two classmates and their injured guide above the timberline, Vale splints a sprained ankle, rations food fairly, and decides when it is safe to cross to a ranger shelter. The story practises FLOSS and blend words like fall, chill, trail and snow, sequencing a rescue plan, and reading clues to infer whether a risky crossing is safe.
